text: As cities continue to grow, finding affordable accommodation has become one of the biggest challenges of urban living. In many major cities, the cost of living has risen so quickly that a housing shortage has pushed rent and property prices to record levels. As a result, some tenants can no longer pay what their landlord asks and are forced to relocate to a cheaper suburb, even if it means a longer commute to work. Meanwhile, gentrification has changed many neighbourhoods, as wealthier residents move in and older, working-class families are pushed out. City centres, filled with skyscrapers, often become overcrowded, while public transport struggles to keep up with demand, leading to serious traffic congestion. Urban planners argue that cities need to grow in a more sustainable way, rather than allowing urban sprawl to destroy natural land nearby. Some governments have started building more affordable housing and improving public transport so that fewer people need a mortgage just to live near their workplace. However, solving the housing crisis will not happen quickly, since it involves difficult questions about who owns property and how cities should be designed for the future.
